    GPU memory math

    After this lesson you can estimate the GPU memory a fine-tune will use, explain why full fine-tuning needs several times the model size, and see exactly where LoRA and mixed precision save memory.

    Level: intermediate Read time: ~10 min Prerequisites: LoRA knobs: rank, alpha, dropout, target modules, QLoRA Verified: 12 Nov 2026

    "Will this fit on my GPU?" is a question you'll ask constantly, and you can answer it with arithmetic. There are four consumers of training memory; knowing them turns out-of-memory errors from mysteries into predictions.

    The four consumers

    • Weights — the parameters themselves. ≈ params × bytes-per-param. At bf16 (2 bytes), a 1B model ≈ 2 GB. (GB here means 109 bytes; 2 GB is 1.86 GiB.)
    • Gradients — one per trainable parameter. In standard mixed-precision training they're kept in fp32: 4 bytes each, ≈ 4 GB for a fully fine-tuned 1B model.
    • Optimizer state — AdamW keeps two extra values per trainable parameter, in fp32, so 8 bytes per trainable parameter — the largest single per-parameter consumer. For a 1B model fully fine-tuned, ≈ 8 GB.
    • Activations — intermediate values from the forward pass, kept for the backward pass. They scale with batch size × sequence length × the model's width and depth. On top sits the logits tensor, batch × sequence × vocabulary, often in fp32: one 2,048-token sequence with a 152k vocabulary is about 1.2 GB of logits on its own. For small models with big vocabularies that is frequently the largest single allocation.

    Why full fine-tuning needs several times the model size

    Standard mixed-precision training with AdamW keeps an fp32 master copy of the weights (4 bytes) and computes with a 16-bit copy (2), plus fp32 gradients (4) and two fp32 Adam moments (8). That is about 16–18 bytes per parameter — 16–18 GB for a fully fine-tuned 1B model before activations (the ZeRO paper counts 16; Hugging Face's memory-anatomy guide counts 18). That's the rule of thumb "full fine-tuning needs several times the model's size in memory", and it's why a model whose weights fit easily can still refuse to train.

    You'll also see "~12 bytes per parameter" quoted: that's pure-bf16 weights and gradients with fp32 Adam moments and no master copy. It's a legitimate setup, but not the default, so label it if you use it.

    Where LoRA saves

    With LoRA the base is frozen, so gradients and optimizer state exist only for the small adapter, and the frozen base can be loaded straight in bf16 at 2 bytes per parameter (or 4-bit with QLoRA). That is the concrete reason LoRA fits where full fine-tuning doesn't. What LoRA does not shrink is activations: backprop still runs through every frozen layer, so activation and logits memory is about the same as in full fine-tuning.

    A measured example: a 30B-parameter mixture-of-experts model with LoRA r=16 on q, k, v and o has 13,369,344 trainable parameters (0.04%), and the adapter's gradients and AdamW state come to about 0.2 GB. The bf16 weights are about 57 GiB, yet the run peaked at about 77 GiB: the other ~20 GiB is activations, logits and runtime overhead. (An MoE needs memory for all its experts, not only the ~3B parameters active per token.)

    Mixed precision and 16-bit weights

    Two different things get called "16-bit", and they save different memory:

    • Loading a frozen base in bf16 (dtype=torch.bfloat16) halves the weight memory compared with fp32. Since nothing trains those weights, no fp32 copy is needed. This is the usual LoRA setup, and what BrewSLM does.
    • Mixed-precision training (bf16/fp16 autocast) computes matmuls in 16-bit while keeping fp32 master weights for the parameters being trained. It mainly saves activation memory and speeds up matmuls; for trained weights it adds a 16-bit copy, so their memory goes up to about 1.5×. bf16 is preferred on modern GPUs for its numerical range, and it's nearly free quality-wise.

    Managing activations

    Activations are the lever you control at run time. For a given model, they grow with batch size × sequence length — how many tokens flow through per step — so the two biggest knobs for fitting a run are exactly those. Gradient checkpointing (next lesson) trades compute to shrink activation memory dramatically. Combined with the earlier lessons: pick max_seq_length from your data, set a per-device batch that fits, and recover the effective batch with gradient accumulation. Leave headroom for the CUDA context (roughly 0.5–1 GB) and allocator fragmentation.

    You now have a mental calculator: weights + gradients + optimizer state + activations (with the logits), scaled by precision. When the sum exceeds your GPU, you get an OOM — and the next lesson is the field guide to surviving exactly that.

    Key terms

    Weights memory
    ≈ params × bytes-per-param (2 bytes at bf16).
    Gradient memory
    One value per trainable parameter (4 bytes each in standard mixed precision).
    Optimizer state
    AdamW's ~8 bytes per trainable parameter — the biggest per-parameter consumer in full fine-tuning, which totals about 16–18 bytes per parameter.
    Activations
    Forward-pass intermediates kept for backprop; scale with batch × sequence length × model width and depth, plus a batch × sequence × vocabulary logits tensor.
    Mixed precision (bf16)
    Computing in 16-bit while keeping fp32 master weights for trained parameters; saves activation memory and time. Loading a frozen base in bf16 is what halves weight memory.
